disease_info: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) is a trauma- and stressor-related condition that emerges within days of exposure to an actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violation, either directly, as a witness, or by learning about it occurring to a close other. It is characterized by a cluster of intrusive recollections, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance, and arousal symptoms that last from 3 days to up to 1 month after the traumatic event and cause significant distress or functional impairment. Clinically, ASD often presents with marked anxiety, sleep disruption, and a sense of being "on edge" or emotionally numb in the immediate aftermath of trauma. It is distinguished from Posttraumatic Stress Disorder primarily by its shorter duration and more prominent acute dissociative features, and it may resolve spontaneously or progress to PTSD if symptoms persist beyond one month.

narrative.personality: She is a highly detail-oriented, anxious young woman who relies on strict routines, careful budgeting, and quiet creative hobbies to feel in control of her life.
narrative.stressor: Two weeks before presentation, Irma was riding home from a late shift at the community health clinic with her older cousin when another car ran a red light and T-boned their vehicle; Irma remained conscious, trapped in the passenger seat, while her cousin was critically injured and had to be extricated in front of her. Accustomed to planning and controlling every detail, she felt utterly helpless as paramedics worked on her cousin and she sat in the wreckage hearing sounds of metal, glass, and sirens, later being discharged from the emergency department with only minor physical injuries. Over the following week, her usual coping routines—journaling, crocheting, meal planning—began to fall apart as she found herself unable to return to her normal bus routes or even walk past busy intersections, and she stopped volunteering at the clinic because she could not tolerate being near the entrance where ambulances arrived. Her mother finally insisted she seek psychiatric care when Irma, exhausted and increasingly irritable, admitted she could not concentrate on basic tasks at home because her mind kept "going back" to the crash whenever she tried to relax or plan her day.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since the car accident, my mind keeps replaying it over and over, even when I don’t want to think about it.”

narrative.personality: She is a quiet, methodical administrator who finds comfort in orderly routines, solitary hobbies like gardening and knitting, and maintaining a calm environment at work and at home.
narrative.stressor: About ten days before seeking help, Linda was supervising an outdoor play session at her early-childhood program when a severe storm rolled in faster than expected and a large tree branch suddenly snapped and fell onto the playground, narrowly missing several children and striking a teaching assistant. As the director, she was the one who had to coordinate the emergency response, call 911, and direct the evacuation while listening to the injured staff member cry out and seeing terrified children clinging to their teachers. In the days that followed, she continued to run the center and manage the incident reports, but she became increasingly uneasy in the building, jumping at hallway noises or when doors slammed, and found herself avoiding walking past the playground or reviewing safety plans in detail because they brought back the moment of the branch falling. Her husband encouraged her to see a psychiatrist when she started startling so intensely at minor sounds at home that she would spill coffee or drop dishes, and she confessed that she felt constantly on edge at work, unable to maintain her usual composed demeanor.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Since that accident at the playground, every little noise makes me jump out of my skin.”

narrative.personality: She is a seasoned, pragmatic paramedic who thrives on structure and leadership in crises but also has a warm, sociable side expressed through theater, community activities, and meticulous preparedness.
narrative.stressor: A week before presentation, Lissa responded with her crew to a multi-vehicle collision on an icy highway where one of the cars belonged to a long-time colleague and friend from her EMS station; she arrived early on scene and immediately recognized his vehicle, then realized he was the unresponsive driver they were attempting to resuscitate. Despite leading a textbook resuscitation effort, he was pronounced dead at the hospital, and Lissa, who was usually proud of her ability to compartmentalize, felt a profound sense of personal failure and shock at losing someone from her own tight-knit EMS community. Over the next several days, she began volunteering to take only non–trauma calls and swapped shifts to avoid driving past that stretch of highway, skipped her usual safety drills and community training sessions, and pulled back from theater rehearsals because the stage lights and mock emergencies reminded her of the crash scene. Her supervisor urged her to seek psychiatric evaluation when she started refusing to get on the ambulance for certain calls, citing vague reasons, and admitted privately that she was going out of her way to avoid anything that might bring back the memory of working on her friend’s body.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since that wreck where my partner died, I’ve been going out of my way to avoid anything that reminds me of that call.”
